opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think "full-stack" is one of those phrases that gets used loosely, so let me say what I mean by it. For us, it means we don't treat the model as one isolated component that gets handed off to someone else to deploy. The data, the pretraining recipe, the post-training and reinforcement learning, the inference infrastructure, and the product people actually touch are all designed together, and each layer constrains the others.

That matters a lot for multimodal reasoning in particular. If you want a model that can look at a chart, a video, or a messy screenshot and reason through it step by step, you can't bolt vision onto a text model at the end and hope it works. You need to think from the start about how the different modalities are represented, how they're mixed in the training data, and what kinds of reasoning traces you want the model to learn. A lot of the hard problems show up at the boundaries between modalities, and if different teams own different pieces, those boundaries are exactly where things fall through the cracks.

The other side is the feedback loop. When you own the product and the serving stack, you can see where the model actually fails for real users. Maybe it's grounding a claim in the right part of an image, or keeping track of state across a long multimodal context. That signal goes straight back into data and training decisions. Reasoning models also spend a lot of compute at inference time, so efficiency isn't something you optimize later. It shapes the architecture and how long you let the model think.

So the short version is that full-stack lets us optimize for the thing we actually care about, useful reasoning in the real world, rather than for a benchmark number at one layer of the system. It's harder and you have to be disciplined about focus, but I think that's where the real progress is going to come from.

r001.rationale: The response says the data, training, inference infrastructure, and product are designed together, with multimodal reasoning guiding choices across those layers.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I say "full-stack," I mean we don't treat the model as a thing that lives in isolation, separate from the hardware it runs on, the data pipeline that feeds it, and the product it eventually ships in. All of those layers should talk to each other, and the design of a multimodal reasoning model changes quite a bit once you take that seriously.

Take the hardware side first. A reasoning model spends most of its compute at inference time, not training time. It's generating long chains of intermediate steps, and if you're reasoning over images, video, or audio, those intermediate representations can be enormous. So we think about the architecture with the serving stack in mind from day one. How do we compress visual tokens before they hit the reasoning loop? Where does the KV cache live, and what does that imply for memory bandwidth? If the infrastructure team and the research team are two different companies, those questions get answered badly, or late. When they sit together, you can co-design: the model gets shaped around what the chips do well, and the serving system gets built around what the model actually needs.

Then there's data. Multimodal reasoning is bottlenecked less by raw data volume and more by the quality of the reasoning traces you can get. Nobody writes down their step-by-step thinking when they look at an X-ray or a circuit diagram. So we have to generate a lot of that, verify it, and feed it back. Owning the whole stack means we can build the verification environments ourselves. If the model is reasoning about a chart, we can render the chart from code and check the answer exactly. If it's reasoning about a physical scene, we can simulate it. That closed loop is only possible when you control the tools, the evaluation, and the training pipeline together.

And finally, the product layer feeds back into all of it. Real users show you where the model fails in ways benchmarks never will. Someone uploads a blurry photo of a handwritten receipt and asks a question that requires three steps of inference. That's the data point that tells you where to invest. If the product team is just a consumer of an API, that signal gets lost. If they're part of the same organization, it becomes training signal within weeks.

So the short version: full-stack lets you make the model smaller, faster, and more grounded than you could if you were optimizing each layer in isolation. The hard part is organizational, not technical. You need people who understand the chip and the user in the same room, and you need to resist the temptation to let any one layer become sacred.

r001.rationale: The response frames hardware, data, serving, evaluation, and product as connected layers that should be co-designed around the multimodal reasoning model, describing shared feedback across the stack.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to design the whole system around the problems we want people to solve. If a model needs to reason across text, images, and audio, that has implications for every layer: the data we collect, how we train it, how we evaluate it, and how we serve it.

For example, understanding a chart isn’t just recognizing the labels. The model has to connect those labels to the visual relationships and then use that information to answer a question. We need training and evaluation that capture that whole task, rather than treating visual understanding and reasoning as separate capabilities.

And then there’s the product side. A model might perform well on a benchmark but take too long to respond or be too expensive for someone to use regularly. A full-stack approach lets us make those tradeoffs together and feed what we learn from actual use back into development. Ultimately, the goal is a system that reasons well across modalities and is useful in practice.

r001.rationale: The response says to design the whole system around multimodal problems and coordinate data collection, training, evaluation, and serving toward that goal.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the full-stack approach means designing the model and the experience together. You start with what you want someone to be able to accomplish, then work backward through the reasoning capabilities, the training data, the infrastructure, and the interface.

For a multimodal reasoning model, that means more than accepting images alongside text. The model needs to connect information across those inputs and use it to solve a problem. If you show it a diagram and ask a question, it should reason about the relationships in the diagram, explain its conclusion, and recognize when something is ambiguous.

The full stack gives you a feedback loop. What you learn from building the product informs what you train and how you evaluate it, while improvements in the model open up new product possibilities. The goal is to make those layers reinforce each other so that better reasoning translates into something useful for the person using it.

r001.rationale: The response describes designing the model, training data, infrastructure, evaluation, and interface together around multimodal reasoning, with those layers reinforcing one another.
